prompt.context: The client is an integrated oil company and controls the entire supply chain from oil wells to gas stations. They have discovered a new automobile fuel that will increase mileage by 30%. It will also cost 10% more to produce the fuel. The fuel is similar to the old fuel in every other way.
prompt.question: What should they do with the new fuel?

clarifying_info.q: How many players are in the industry?
clarifying_info.a: There are 5 players in the industry including our client. They all have equal market share.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any environmental concerns or advantages with the new fuel?
clarifying_info.a: No special environmental concerns or advantages from the new fuel.
Under no circumstances can the client capture more than 10% of the market due to capacity constraint.

clarifying_info.q: What are the margins on the current fuel?

framework: Demand issues — estimate market size and likely demand for the new fuel; assess price elasticity
Capacity issues — client is capped at 10% market share due to production constraints
Internal issues — assess whether the new fuel can be produced on the same machinery and distributed through the same channels
Competitive analysis — how will the 4 other players respond to the new fuel launch
Environmental issues — any regulatory or environmental considerations
Alternate uses of the fuel — explore whether the fuel has applications beyond private automobiles

questions.prompt: How should the new fuel be priced relative to the old fuel, and what would the gross margins be?
questions.guidance: A strong answer indexes the new fuel's price to the value it delivers (30% more mileage = effectively 30% cheaper per mile), so the rational ceiling is ~$1.30 if old fuel is $1. With production cost 10% higher ($0.99 vs $0.90), the margin jumps significantly. Candidate should walk through the arithmetic explicitly.

math.setup: Assume old fuel price = $1.00, old fuel cost = $0.90 (10% margin). New fuel gives 30% more mileage so a customer pays up to $1.30 for equivalent value. New fuel costs 10% more to produce: $0.90 × 1.10 = $0.99.
steps: Old fuel: price $1.00, cost $0.90, gross profit $0.10, margin 10%
math.answer: New fuel gross margin is approximately 25%, compared to 10% on the old fuel — a 2.5× improvement.

questions.prompt: Estimate the total weekly fuel demand in the market.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure a top-down guesstimate: population → households → cars → gallons per week. Show clear assumptions at each step.

math.setup: Use US population of ~300 million, average household size 4, one car per household, estimate weekly fuel consumption per car.
math.answer: Total weekly market demand is approximately 1.5 billion gallons per week.

questions.prompt: How might competitors retaliate, and how does the client's capacity constraint affect the competitive dynamic?
questions.guidance: Strong answer recognizes two scenarios: (1) competitors price-match or undercut on old fuel, triggering a price war; (2) because the client is capped at 10% market share, competitors may rationally choose not to respond with a price war since the threat to their volume is limited. The client, with 2.5× better margins on the new fuel, is better positioned to win a price war if one starts.

math.setup: Competitors would drop old fuel price until variable costs are covered (break-even pricing) if they retaliate. But since the client cannot exceed 10% market share, the competitive displacement is bounded.
steps: Client maximum share gain = 10% of market
Competitor minimum share loss = spread across 4 players ≈ 2.5% each
Marginal impact on competitor revenue is small, so a price war is not necessarily rational for competitors
Client with 25% margin vs. competitor 10% margin can sustain a price war longer
math.answer: Competitors are unlikely to initiate a price war because the client's capacity cap limits market share displacement; if they do, the client's superior margins give it staying power.

questions.prompt: (Complication) There are two distinct markets: private sector and government. The government buys 10% of total market and buys equally from all 5 players. Should the client sell only to the government? What effect would this have on prices?
questions.guidance: A strong answer notes that selling exclusively to the government segments the market and avoids triggering a private-sector price war entirely. The government is a captive, non-price-sensitive buyer that already sources equally from all players; selling the new fuel only into this channel avoids competitive retaliation in the main market. Candidate should also note that removing supply from the private market could push private-sector prices up.

math.setup: Government buys 10% of 1.5B gallons/week = 150M gallons/week, split equally among 5 players = 30M gallons/week per player.
steps: If client sells new fuel only to government, private sector sees no change in supply from client (client continues old fuel or withdraws from private sector)
No competitive retaliation because private-sector incumbents are undisturbed
Higher margins captured on 30M gallons/week without price war risk
math.answer: Selling exclusively to the government is strategically sensible: it captures the higher-margin new fuel revenue while avoiding any private-sector price war.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the strategic and operational issues the client should consider before launching the new fuel?

categories.name: Demand
ideas: Price elasticity of automobile fuel
Consumer willingness to pay a premium for better mileage
Marketing and awareness needed to shift consumer behavior
Fleet vs. individual consumer demand differences

categories.name: Capacity
ideas: Client hard-capped at 10% market share by production capacity
Opportunity to expand capacity before competitors discover similar fuel
Prioritize highest-margin customer segments given limited supply

categories.name: Internal / Operations
ideas: Can new fuel be produced on existing refinery equipment?
Does it require new storage tanks or dispensing equipment at gas stations?
Distribution channel compatibility
Employee training and safety requirements

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Can competitors replicate the fuel? How long would it take?
First-mover advantage and IP / trade secret protection
Risk of price war on old fuel as a retaliatory tactic
Competitor capacity to also launch improved fuels

categories.name: Pricing Strategy
ideas: Value-based pricing at $1.30 captures full consumer surplus
Penetration pricing slightly above old fuel to gain share quickly (constrained by capacity cap)
Premium brand positioning for the new fuel
Bundling or loyalty programs at gas stations

categories.name: Environmental / Regulatory
ideas: Any emissions differences requiring regulatory approval?
Government incentives for higher-efficiency fuels?
Future regulatory tailwinds that favor the new fuel

categories.name: Alternate Uses
ideas: Industrial or commercial fleet applications
Aviation or marine fuel adaptations
Government / military procurement (links to the complication scenario)
Licensing the formula to other refiners

recommendation: Launch the new fuel at a value-based price of approximately $1.30 per gallon (assuming old fuel at $1.00), capturing ~25% gross margins versus 10% on old fuel

Prioritize selling to the government channel first, since the government purchases 10% of the market and buys equally from all players — this avoids triggering a private-sector price war while testing the market
Expand capacity if feasible to capture more than the current 10% market cap over time
risks: Competitors replicate the fuel formula, eroding the margin advantage
Competitors retaliate with price cuts on old fuel in the private market
Capacity constraint limits revenue upside; competitors benefit if new fuel drives up private-sector prices
Consumer inertia or skepticism may slow adoption despite better mileage
next_steps: Assess IP protection options (trade secrets, patents) to extend the competitive window
Model capacity expansion costs versus incremental margin to evaluate investment case
Conduct consumer research on willingness to pay and adoption timeline
Evaluate government procurement process and timeline for the new fuel
